For chemistry. .

Option 1.. Potassium Permanganate (used as a disinfectant) mixed with Glycerol (a thick clear liquid).

Both should be available from a chemist/pharmacy/drug store.

Put a couple of teaspoons of Potassium Permanaganate in a small dish. Pour on about a teaspoon of Glycerol. The glycerol will disolve the Potassium Permanganate forming a thick black bubbling ooze. Then small purple flames will appear (up to 5cm) accompanied by massive amounts of white smoke.

For obvious reasons do this outside, and take appropriate safety precautions (goggles gloves etc) especially with kids around.

Hydrogen Peroxide and yeast. You can get a weak solution of Hydrogen Peroxide in the form of a hair lightening product from a pharmacy. Yeast you can buy at any supermarket. Mix together with dishwashing liquid to make a disturbing amount of bubbles..

Here is my a arguement against living in a simulation, and it's fairly simple. Irrational Numbers. There would have to be constraints built into a simulation, unbreakable rules such as the laws of thermal dynamics or the speed of light. Those constraints would preclude the concept of infinity.
T H E L E A D P I L L

If a contemporary scientist were somehow to acquire the means to run such a simulation, and if simulated beings were accorded similar rights to even animals in the real world, it seems likely that they would be forbidden from doing so by their ethics committee unless the experimenters had a very good reason. What reason would justify the enactment or re-enactment of World War II?

The question then is whether anything learned by running a simulation could be learned by other means. A simulation of World War II might be run to find out, for example, the probability that the allies win, given some probability distribution on the initial conditions. In fact, many runs of such a simulation would be required for this. This is essentially counting the number of solutions of a huge boolean circuit that runs the simulation and returns "win" or "lose". If the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_time_hypothesis) is FALSE (currently unknown) then it would be more efficient to use approximate counting instead (https://people.csail.mit.edu/dmoshkov/courses/adv-comp/scribe22.pdf P 4) (some assumptions about the presence of good local approximations to the probability might be required, or some more sophisticated approach). This would be more efficient than running countless simulations, and this efficiency might get it past the ethics committee: if the computation is more efficient than some large number of simulations, it is not traceable to any particular simulation run, and so is not a disguised simulation that involves subjecting simulated populations to countless different versions of World War II.

So the question of whether our descendants might wish to run such simulations, or might outlaw them as we have outlawed bear-baiting, might be affected by currently unresolved questions in computer science, just as the legal status of experiments on animals is currently affected by whether accurate alternatives to experimenting on live animals are available.
